title: How long, Catiline?
saying: Quō ūsque tandem abūtēre, Catilīna, patientiā nostrā?
author: Cicero

source_text: quo usque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra? quam diu etiam furor iste tuus nos eludet? quem ad finem sese effrenata iactabit audacia? nihilne te nocturnum praesidium Palati, nihil urbis vigiliae, nihil timor populi, nihil concursus bonorum omnium, nihil hic munitissimus habendi senatus locus, nihil horum ora voltusque moverunt? patere tua consilia non sentis, constrictam iam horum omnium scientia teneri coniurationem tuam non vides? quid proxima, quid superiore nocte egeris, ubi fueris, quos convocaveris, quid consili ceperis quem nostrum ignorare arbitraris? O tempora, o mores! senatus haec intellegit, consul videt; hic tamen vivit.
excerpt_note: Section 1.1 complete and the opening of 1.2, up to "hic tamen vivit." The Perseus file prints sentence-initial words in lower case (it tags them as regularized), so the speech begins "quo usque"; this text keeps the letters exactly. Clark's apparatus notes (e.g. that some manuscripts omit nos) are left out.

translation: Just how far, Catiline, will you go in abusing our patience? How much longer will that madness of yours keep making fools of us? What limit is there to the swaggering of your unbridled recklessness? Has nothing moved you: not the night guard on the Palatine, not the patrols in the city, not the people's fear, not the rallying of every loyal citizen, not this heavily defended place where the senate is meeting, not the faces and looks of the men here? Do you not realize that your plans are out in the open? Do you not see that your conspiracy is already caught and held, because everyone here knows about it? What you did last night and the night before, where you were, whom you called together, what plan you settled on: which of us do you suppose does not know? What times! What morals! The senate understands all this, the consul sees it; and yet this man is still alive.
translation_note: Abūtēre is the future of the deponent abūtor, with the alternative ending -ēre for -ēris; it takes an ablative (patientiā). Quō ūsque means "up to what point". In Ō tempora, ō mōrēs! the accusatives are exclamations. The repeated nihil ("not at all") is used as an adverb, with all six subjects sharing the one verb mōvērunt. Bonī, "the good", is Cicero's word for loyal, propertied citizens on his side.

essay.t: Cicero was consul in 63 BC; Britannica says the optimates had backed his election because they feared the revolutionary ideas of his rival, Catiline.
Catiline planned armed risings and arson, and Cicero struggled to convince the senate of the danger until the "last decree" was passed on 22 October.

Sallust, the other main narrative source, says Catiline came into the senate to look innocent, and that Cicero, either afraid of his presence or angry, delivered a brilliant speech useful to the state, which he afterwards wrote out and published.

That last detail matters. In a letter to Atticus of 60 BC, Cicero says he is assembling a collection of "consular speeches", on the model of Demosthenes' Philippics, and lists among them the speech "when I drove Catiline out".
So the text we read is the version Cicero chose to publish; how closely it matches what he said on the day cannot be checked.
In my reading, the published speech casts him as the watchful consul who sees everything, as in the line "the consul sees".
The arrested conspirators were debated in the senate, where, in Sallust's account, Caesar warned against deciding in anger.
The senate followed Cato. Lentulus was taken down into the Tullianum, a dark, foul cell about twelve feet underground, and strangled with a noose; four others were executed the same way.
Catiline died fighting in the field; Sallust says he was found far from his own men among enemy corpses, still breathing.

Britannica describes the executions as carried out "on Cicero's responsibility" and says he announced them with one word, vixerunt, "they have lived"; the anecdote is not in Sallust, and I have not traced its ancient source.

That responsibility came back to him. When Clodius became tribune in 58 BC and Pompey refused help, Cicero left Rome, and Clodius passed a law of doubtful legality declaring him an exile; Pompey and Milo later helped secure his recall.
The famous cry, then, survives in a speech its author shaped for readers as well as for the senate.

questions.q: According to Sallust, what did Cicero do with this speech after giving it?
options: He wrote it out and published it
He had it carved on bronze

questions.q: What does Sallust say happened to Lentulus?
options: He was strangled in the Tullianum
He died in battle beside Catiline

questions.q: Why did the executions later cause trouble for Cicero?
options: Clodius passed a law declaring him an exile
